correctness.rationale: Every moment is defined for uniform three-dimensional volume and a fixed symmetry-centered origin. Coordinate sign-pair flips and permutations give the complete quartic polynomial for the tetrahedron, cube and octahedron; exact Dirichlet and independent product integrations yield their coefficients. Exact triangular-face moments and a volume-preserving radial pyramid disintegration give a single rational expression in face shape parameters that simplifies to all five displayed radial ratios. Averaging degree-two and degree-four characters over the 60-element icosahedral rotation group proves the remaining fourth-order tensors are isotropic. Sharp angular extrema follow from 1/3<=sum(u_i^4)<=1. The package checker symbolically replays each identity and directly samples uniformly in all five triangulated solids as a diagnostic.
risks: The use of full-volume, rather than surface/vertex, measures is essential.
The stochastic finite verification is not substituted for any exact or quantified proof.

It does not state the normalized angular polynomial coefficients, the tetrahedron--cube equality, the five exact radial kurtoses, or the sharp angular ranges. Earlier materially inspected sources either compute second-order tetrahedral inertia or establish Platonic volume geometry and disintegration, not this quantified rank-four spectrum. value.rationale: The known general symmetry classification answers only whether the fourth moment depends on direction; high-order inertia has explicit geometric and engineering motivation. The exact five-body normalized tensor table answers the natural next question of how strongly each case varies. It yields all extremizing directions and values, an unexpected tetrahedron--cube angular identity, and a separate exact radial kurtosis classification. The five Platonic solids form the complete natural finite set of three-dimensional regular convex polyhedra, not an arbitrary collection of isolated numerical test cases.
risks: The contribution is a canonical complete exact classification, not an extremal theorem for arbitrary convex bodies.
